question: An HR team has a Claude-drafted consultation letter that will be sent to forty staff whose roles are at risk, and the wording is governed by employment law. Which sequence is correct?
options: A) Judge the stakes of the letter, then name the reviewer it requires, then have that reviewer check it against the consultation policy, then send it once approval is recorded.
B) Record who approved the wording, then send the letter to the forty staff, then check it against the consultation policy, then have the HR lead read it.
C) Send the letter to the forty staff, then have the HR lead read it, then check it against the consultation policy, then record who approved the wording.
D) Check the letter against the consultation policy, then send it to the forty staff, then judge the stakes of what was sent, then name a reviewer to look over it carefully afterwards.
correct_answers: A) Judge the stakes of the letter, then name the reviewer it requires, then have that reviewer check it against the consultation policy, then send it once approval is recorded.
explanations: Correct. The stakes are high, regulated and irreversible, so the level of scrutiny is decided first, a named person is made accountable for the review, the check is made against the governing policy, and despatch happens only after recorded approval.
Recording an approval before anyone has reviewed the letter documents a sign-off that never happened, and the substantive checks still fall after the letter has already gone out.

Sending first makes every later step a post-mortem. A consultation letter cannot be recalled from forty recipients, so review carried out after despatch cannot prevent the harm it is meant to prevent.

Checking against the policy first is sensible, but sending before any named person has reviewed the letter or the stakes have been weighed removes the human review gate exactly where irreversibility demands it.
